title: How to Reduce Bathroom Condensation Before It Becomes a Bigger Problem
description: A simple ventilation routine for reducing foggy mirrors, damp surfaces and the conditions that let moisture linger after a shower.
image_alt: Clean bright bathroom with shower and ventilation
body_html:
Steam on the mirror is normal. Moisture that stays on walls, ceilings and fabrics for hours is the part worth fixing. The goal is not to make a bathroom perfectly dry; it is to move humid air out efficiently.

Start ventilation before the room gets saturated

Turn the extractor on when the shower starts, not only after it ends. Keep the bathroom door mostly closed while showering so humid air does not spread through the home.

Give the fan time to finish the job

Leave the extractor running after the shower. The exact time depends on the room and fan, but the practical test is whether the mirror and wet surfaces are clearing steadily rather than staying coated.

Use the window as a tool, not the only solution

If the bathroom has a window and outdoor conditions are suitable, opening it can help exchange air. In cold or very humid weather, however, a properly working extractor may be more useful than leaving a window open for a long time.

Check the fan itself

Dust on the grille can reduce airflow. Switch the fan off, clean the grille according to its instructions, and check that the airflow is actually moving outside rather than simply circulating inside a ceiling void.

A five-minute routine

  • Run the extractor during the shower.
  • Keep the bathroom door mostly closed.
  • Continue ventilation afterward.
  • Wipe persistent standing water from surfaces.
  • Clean the fan grille regularly.

If condensation remains unusually heavy despite good ventilation, look for leaks, failed exhaust ducting or another moisture source rather than simply running the fan longer.
